objective: Prediction formula: valid predictions combine personal cultural background, lived experience, and explicit clues from the text/visual material.；Prediction uses same logic as inference, but focuses on future outcomes rather than past/present.；Predictions must be evidence-based educated guesses, not wild guesses.

learningGoals.statement: Make evidence-based predictions by combining cultural background, personal experience, and textual/visual clues.
Distinguish between inference and prediction based on time focus.
Analyze graphic texts by integrating observed visual details with personal knowledge to form valid conclusions.

knowledgeNodes.definition: Predictions are evidence-based educated guesses about future outcomes, combining personal cultural background, lived experience, and explicit clues from the text or visual material. They use the same logic as inferences but focus on future events.

questions.successCriteria: Student selects option B, showing understanding that predictions must be based on evidence from the text/visual.

questions.alignmentNote: Making predictions using text/visual clues is a core reading strategy under A3.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student recognizes that predictions must be supported by explicit clues from the source material.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think any plausible guess is valid, even if it lacks basis in the text or visual.
questions.stem: Which of the following predictions is evidence-based?

options.label: A
options.text: The character will win because I want him to.
options.feedbackWrong: This prediction is based on personal desire, not on clues from the text or visual.

options.label: B
options.text: Based on the dark clouds and the character grabbing an umbrella, it will rain.
options.feedbackWrong: This prediction uses specific visual clues (dark clouds, umbrella) to make a logical guess.

options.label: C
options.text: The story will be boring because I don't like this genre.
options.feedbackWrong: This prediction is based on personal opinion, not on evidence from the text.

options.label: D
options.text: Something exciting will happen because it's a movie.
options.feedbackWrong: This prediction is a vague assumption about the genre, not based on specific evidence.

questions.successCriteria: Student identifies the statement as an inference, showing understanding that inference focuses on past/present conclusions.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Distinguishing inference from prediction is part of using reading strategies under A3.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding that inference draws conclusions about what is already implied, while prediction anticipates future events.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think inference and prediction are identical processes.
questions.stem: After reading a story, you say: 'The character has already decided to run away.' This statement is an example of:

options.label: A
options.feedbackWrong: Correct. Inference draws a conclusion about something that has already happened or is implied.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: Prediction focuses on future outcomes. This sentence describes a decision already made, indicating inference.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: The statement is about a past decision, not about a future event, so it cannot be a prediction.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: The statement is a conclusion based on text clues, so it fits the definition of inference.

questions.successCriteria: Student selects option B, demonstrating awareness that the cultural context of the setting must be considered.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Considering cultural background is part of making informed predictions under A3.
questions.stemIntent: Check awareness that predictions must account for the cultural context of the text, not just the reader's own culture.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may assume their own cultural norms universally apply, ignoring the text's cultural setting.
questions.stem: When predicting the next scene in a film set in a rural Chinese village, which factor should you most carefully consider?

options.label: A
options.text: Your personal experience growing up in a city
options.feedbackWrong: Personal experience is important, but it should be combined with the culture of the setting, not replace it.

options.label: B
options.text: Cultural practices common in rural China
options.feedbackWrong: Correct. The cultural background of the story's setting is crucial for making accurate predictions.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: Physical appearances provide clues, but cultural context helps interpret them properly.

options.label: D
options.text: A wild guess based on no evidence
options.feedbackWrong: Predictions must be evidence-based, not random guesses.

questions.successCriteria: Student makes a plausible future prediction and explicitly references at least two of the three factors (cultural background, personal experience, text/visual clues).
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Applying the three factors to make predictions demonstrates use of reading strategies under A3.
questions.stemIntent: Check ability to integrate personal experience and other factors to produce a reasoned prediction.
questions.commonMisconception: Student may make a prediction without referencing personal experience, relying only on visual clues or irrelevant experience.
questions.stem: Look at the image of children playing on a log in a river. Write one prediction about what might happen next. Explain how you used at least two of the three prediction factors (cultural background, personal experience, text/visual clues) to form your prediction.
questions.rubric: Student makes a plausible future prediction that is directly tied to at least two of the three factors. For example: 'The children will fall off because I have seen kids lose balance on wet logs (personal experience) and their postures look unsteady (visual clue).' (Accept any similar use of factors.)
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: I predict one child will slip and fall into the river because from personal experience I know logs get slippery when wet, and the visual shows the children laughing and pushing each other, making the log wobble. Also, in some cultures, playing near water is common, but safety is often overlooked.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option on diagnostic question Q1.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think any plausible guess is valid as a prediction, even if it lacks basis in the text or visual clues. They do not understand that predictions must be evidence-based educated guesses combining personal background, experience, and explicit clues.

miniLesson.explain: Predictions are not wild guesses. They are educated guesses based on evidence from the text or visual material, your own experiences, and cultural background. You must point to specific clues that support your prediction. A valid prediction combines personal cultural background, lived experience, and explicit clues from the text/visual.
miniLesson.example: For instance, seeing dark clouds and a character grabbing an umbrella, you can predict it will rain because the visual gives you direct clues. That's evidence-based, not a wild guess.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: A prediction without evidence is like a ship without a sail – it goes nowhere. Always anchor your prediction with clues from the text or image.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following is an evidence-based prediction?
A) 'I think the character will win because I like him.'
B) 'Based on the character's worried expression and the ticking clock, I predict he will miss the deadline.'
Look at the image of a firefighter running into a burning building. The firefighter is holding a child. Make one evidence-based prediction about what will happen next. Use at least one visual clue.
guidedPractice.answer: I predict the firefighter will carry the child to safety because the firefighter is moving away from the flames and holding the child protectively.

guidedPractice.prompt: Think of a story or movie you know. Describe one scene and make a prediction about a future event in that story. Explain what clues from the story and your own experience led to that prediction.
guidedPractice.answer: In the movie 'The Lion King', after Mufasa dies, I predicted Simba would eventually return to take his place as king because the story showed Simba's growth and his sense of responsibility. I've seen similar hero's journey stories where the protagonist returns after a loss.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option on diagnostic question Q2, which tests the ability to distinguish inference from prediction.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student does not understand that inference draws conclusions about past/present events while prediction anticipates future outcomes. They may think the two processes are identical or interchangeable.

miniLesson.explain: Prediction and inference both use evidence from the text or visuals, but they differ in time focus. Inference draws a conclusion about what is already implied or has happened (past/present). Prediction anticipates what will happen next (future). For example, seeing dark clouds and an umbrella, you can infer that the character is prepared for rain, and predict that it will rain soon.
miniLesson.example: From the short film 'Lather and Nothing Else', an inference is 'the barber is a secret revolutionary' (based on his internal thoughts). A prediction would be 'the barber will not kill the captain' (based on his character and the situation).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Inference = 'what happened?' (past/present). Prediction = 'what will happen?' (future). Both use the same evidence, but answer different questions.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following: 'The character sighed and put down the phone.' Which is an inference? A) She will call someone else. B) The conversation ended. C) She is angry. D) She will cry.
Explain why the sentence 'The detective has already found the clue' is an inference, not a prediction. Provide a prediction that could follow from this inference.
guidedPractice.answer: It is an inference because it states a conclusion about an event that has already occurred (finding the clue). A possible prediction could be 'The detective will solve the case soon.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the image of children playing on a log in a river. Write one inference about the current situation and one prediction about what might happen next. Explain how each uses the same visual clues but differ in time focus.
guidedPractice.answer: Inference: The children are playing carelessly because they are laughing and the log is unstable (clues: body language, log position). Prediction: One child will fall into the water because the log may tip over. The inference describes the present behavior; the prediction anticipates a future outcome.

reteachModules.trigger: Student predicts based solely on visual clues or personal experience, ignoring the cultural setting of the text.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student assumes their own cultural norms apply universally, not recognizing that the story's cultural background may lead to different outcomes.

miniLesson.explain: Predictions must consider the cultural background of the story's setting. Cultural norms, traditions, and values influence characters' actions and story outcomes. The three factors are: cultural background, personal experience, and text/visual clues. Ignoring cultural context can lead to inappropriate predictions.
miniLesson.example: Children playing on a log in a river: if you ignore cultural background, you might predict they will fall (based on your own experience). But in some cultures, children are trained to balance on logs from a young age, so they might not fall.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Culture is context: your culture is not the only one.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this sentence: 'In the village, everyone gathers for the Spring Festival Gala.' Based on cultural background, what is a likely prediction about what people will do next?
guidedPractice.answer: They will watch the TV program together and celebrate.

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the image of a firefighter. The text says the story is set in a country where firefighters are highly respected. Predict how the community will react to the firefighter arriving.
guidedPractice.answer: The community will show gratitude and offer help because respecting firefighters is a cultural norm in that setting.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a short film set in a culture where barbers are considered secret keepers, what might happen when a barber recognizes a dangerous customer? Use cultural background, personal experience, and visual clues from the lesson example 'Lather and Nothing Else'.
guidedPractice.answer: The barber might pretend not to recognize the customer to protect his own safety, as the cultural role of barbers as confidants would make it dangerous to reveal knowledge. This combines cultural understanding with the tension from visual clues.

reteachModules.trigger: Student's open-ended response on the diagnostic prediction task did not include personal experience as a factor.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Personal lived experience is unnecessary for making predictions; only text/visual clues matter.

miniLesson.explain: Valid predictions combine three factors: cultural background, personal lived experience, and explicit clues from the text/visual material. Your personal experience helps you interpret clues and imagine realistic outcomes. For example, if you see children playing on a wet log in a river, your experience with slippery surfaces helps you predict someone might slip.
miniLesson.example: In the 'Children Playing on a Log in River' image, a student who has fallen from a wet log (personal experience) would predict a child slipping, while a student who has only seen stable logs might predict they stay safe.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think '3 Legs of a Stool' — prediction needs cultural background, personal experience, AND text/visual clues. Missing one makes it wobbly.

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the image of a child reaching for a cookie jar on a high shelf. Make one prediction and explain how your personal experience helps you make it.
guidedPractice.answer: Prediction: The child will knock over a glass. Personal experience: I once tried to grab something high and accidentally knocked things over.

guidedPractice.prompt: In the 'Family Watching Spring Festival Gala' image, predict one thing the family might do after the show. Use visual clues and your personal experience of family gatherings to support your answer.
guidedPractice.answer: Prediction: They will take a group photo. Visual clue: They are sitting close with smiles. Personal experience: My family always takes photos at gatherings.

guidedPractice.prompt: From the short film 'Lather and Nothing Else', predict what the barber will do when the captain leaves. Explain how you used the captain's dialogue (visual clue) and your own experience with trust or fear to form the prediction.
guidedPractice.answer: Prediction: The barber will quickly leave or hide. Visual clue: The captain's suspicious tone. Personal experience: When I sense danger, I remove myself from the situation.

reteachModules.trigger: Student responds to an inference question by merely describing visible content without synthesizing clues with personal knowledge.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks that simply restating what is visible already counts as an inference, not realizing that inference requires combining observed details with background knowledge to form a new conclusion that goes beyond the literal text or image.

miniLesson.explain: An inference is not just describing what you see; it’s using what you see plus what you already know to figure out something new. For example, if you see a person holding an umbrella and dark clouds, you don’t just say ‘I see an umbrella and clouds’—you infer ‘It’s going to rain.’ The inference combines the visual clues (umbrella, dark clouds) with personal knowledge (umbrellas are for rain, dark clouds mean rain) to reach a new conclusion.
miniLesson.example: Look at the firefighter image from class. Observations: the firefighter is crouching, holding a hose, and there is smoke in the background. Personal knowledge: firefighters extinguish fires. Inference: the firefighter is about to put out a fire. Notice the inference is NOT ‘I see a firefighter with a hose’ (that’s just description). It’s the new idea that goes beyond what’s directly visible.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Inference = Clues + Your Brain = New Idea. If you’re only describing, you haven’t inferred yet.

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at this statement about a picture: 'There is a boy holding a baseball bat and looking at a ball.' Is this a description or an inference? Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: This is a description because it only states what is visible (boy, bat, ball, looking). It does not combine these clues with personal knowledge to create a new conclusion, such as 'the boy is about to hit the ball.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Describe the visual: A woman is standing at a bus stop, looking at her watch, and there is a car approaching in the distance. Make one inference based on these clues. In your answer, state your inference and explain which clues and personal knowledge you used.
guidedPractice.answer: Inference: The woman is waiting for the bus and is worried she might miss it. I used the visual clue 'looking at her watch' and the clue 'at a bus stop' combined with personal knowledge that people check time when they are waiting and anxious about being late. The car is irrelevant; the key clues are watch and bus stop.

guidedPractice.prompt: Consider this graphic text: a cartoon panel shows a character looking at a messy room with a vacuum cleaner in the corner and a calendar on the wall with a date circled. Make an inference about what the character is likely thinking. Use at least two types of clues (e.g., emphasized content, body language, unusual details) and your own experience to support your inference.
guidedPractice.answer: Inference: The character is thinking they need to clean the room before the circled date (maybe a parent’s visit or a party). Clues: the vacuum cleaner is emphasized (large size, bright color) and the circled date on the calendar is an unusual detail; body language: character’s hands on hips suggests frustration or determination. Personal experience: when I have a messy room and see a vacuum, I think about cleaning; seeing a circled date reminds me of deadlines. So the combination leads to the inference about planning to clean.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option on Q6 of the diagnostic, indicating they provided a location description without specific supporting details from the graphic text.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks that simply naming the location (e.g., 'it's a park') is sufficient for analysis, without referencing specific visual elements (colors, objects, people's actions) and personal knowledge to make a valid inference.

miniLesson.explain: When analyzing a graphic text, a location description is not enough. You must include specific visual details you see and connect them with your own knowledge to form a deeper conclusion. For example, instead of saying 'a family room', say 'the room has a large TV showing a Spring Festival Gala and the family is seated together smiling, suggesting a cultural celebration.' Use the three types of visual clues: emphasized content (what stands out), body language/movement (postures, actions), and unusual details (anything that seems odd or significant). Then combine with your cultural background or personal experience to explain what the image means.
miniLesson.example: Look at the image of a family watching the Spring Festival Gala. Instead of just saying 'It's a living room,' a detailed inference would be: 'The large TV prominently shows the Spring Festival Gala (emphasized content), the family members are sitting close to each other with smiles (body language), and there are red decorations (unusual detail). These clues, combined with my knowledge of Chinese New Year traditions, tell me this is a family celebrating together during the holiday.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: DIVE into details! Describe what you see, Identify clues, Verify with personal knowledge, Explain the meaning. Don't just name the location—DIVE deeper!

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the image of children playing on a log in a river. Write one sentence that describes the location with at least two specific visual details.
guidedPractice.answer: The children are sitting on a log that is partially submerged in a muddy river, with one child pointing downstream.

guidedPractice.prompt: Using the same image, now make an inference about the location and explain how you combined visual clues with personal knowledge.
guidedPractice.answer: The log being wet and the children's bare feet suggest they are in a rural area where playing in the river is common. I know from my own experience that logs can be slippery, so their tense postures indicate they are trying to keep balance.

guidedPractice.prompt: Look at the image of a family watching the Spring Festival Gala. Write a paragraph that analyzes the scene in detail, using all three types of visual clues (emphasized content, body language, unusual details) and your cultural knowledge to form a conclusion about the family's experience.
guidedPractice.answer: The image shows a family gathered in a cozy room. The emphasized content is the large TV screen displaying the Spring Festival Gala, a traditional Chinese New Year broadcast. The family's body language—leaning forward with smiles and clapping hands—shows they are engaged and happy. Unusual details include red lanterns and couplets on the walls, which are symbols of good luck. Combining these clues with my knowledge of Chinese culture, I conclude this family is celebrating the New Year together, enjoying a shared cultural tradition that strengthens family bonds.

questions.stem: Which of the following predictions is evidence-based?
options: I predict the character will find treasure because I want a happy ending.
I predict the character will open the door because they are reaching for the handle and looking nervous.

questions.stem: Look at the image of a child holding a half-eaten apple and frowning. Make one evidence-based prediction about what might happen next. Explain what clues you used.
questions.rubric: Student must mention at least one visual clue (e.g., half-eaten apple, frowning) and make a plausible future outcome (e.g., the child will not finish the apple, or will ask for something else). The prediction must be grounded in the clue, not a wild guess.

questions.stem: Read the following scenario: 'A student sees a test on the teacher's desk with a red mark on one paper. The teacher is frowning.' Which of the following is a prediction based on this scenario?
options: The student failed the test.
The student will receive a low grade.
The teacher is grading papers.
The test was hard.

questions.stem: Consider a photograph showing a crowded subway car with a person holding a baby and looking at the door. Provide one inference about the current situation and one prediction about what might happen next. Then explain how the inference and prediction differ in terms of time focus.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies an inference (conclusion about present/past, e.g., 'The person with the baby wants to get off') and a prediction (future event, e.g., 'The doors will open and they will exit'). Explanation must mention that inference describes what is happening or has happened, while prediction anticipates a future event.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For Q1, select option B (index 1). For Q2, inference and prediction must be logically consistent with scenario and explanation must clearly distinguish time focus (past/present vs future).

questions.stem: You see an image of a group of people bowing deeply to an elderly person. The story is set in a culture where bowing is a sign of deep respect. What is the most likely prediction about the elderly person's response?
options: The elderly person will ignore them.
The elderly person will bow back respectfully.
The elderly person will run away.
The elderly person will laugh.

questions.stem: Read the following: In a story set in a culture where silence is valued during meals, a family is having dinner. Predict what will happen if a child starts talking loudly. Explain how cultural background influences your prediction.
questions.rubric: Student predicts a consequence that reflects the cultural norm (e.g., child is corrected or reprimanded) and explicitly states that the cultural value of silence shapes the prediction.

retestCards.passRule: Answer q1 correctly, and for q2 mention cultural background as a factor in the prediction.

questions.stem: You see a person wearing a heavy coat and carrying an umbrella on a cloudy day. Which prediction best shows how personal experience helps make a valid prediction?
options: The person will go to work because it is a weekday.
The person will open the umbrella because I have done the same when rain started.
The person will take a taxi because the clouds look dark.
The person will stay home because the weather is bad.

questions.stem: Look at the image: a child is reaching for a cookie jar on a high shelf, and there is a glass on the edge nearby. Predict what might happen next. In your answer, state the prediction and explain how your personal experience (from your own life) helps you make that prediction.
questions.rubric: Prediction must be a plausible future event. Explanation must include a specific personal experience that relates to the situation (e.g., reaching for something high, knocking things over). Score 1 for clear prediction + relevant personal experience. Score 0 otherwise.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For Q2, the response must explicitly mention personal experience or lived experience as a factor in the prediction reasoning.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an inference, not a description?
options: A woman is holding an umbrella and there are dark clouds.
The woman is wearing a raincoat and standing under a bus shelter.
It is going to rain because the woman has an umbrella and the sky is dark.
The woman is looking up at the sky.

questions.stem:
Look at this scene: A student is sitting at a desk with a laptop open, a half-eaten sandwich, and a clock showing 11:30 PM. The student is rubbing their eyes.

Make one inference about the student. In your answer, state your inference and explain which clues and personal knowledge you used.
questions.rubric: Student states a reasonable inference (e.g., 'The student is studying late at night and is tired.'). They must mention at least one visual clue (e.g., clock showing 11:30 PM, rubbing eyes, half-eaten sandwich) and one piece of personal knowledge (e.g., people rub eyes when tired, eating late can mean studying). Inference must go beyond description. If answer is purely descriptive (e.g., 'The student is at a desk with a laptop and sandwich'), it does not pass.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer the single-choice question correctly AND submit an open-ended response that makes a valid inference supported by at least one clue and personal knowledge (not merely describing).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a well-supported inference from a graphic text?
options: It's a park.
The park has children playing on a slide and a mother watching from a bench; their smiles suggest they are enjoying a sunny afternoon.
I think they are happy.
The park is big.

cards.question: Which of the following predictions is evidence-based?
options: The character will win because I want him to.
Based on the dark clouds and the character grabbing an umbrella, it will rain.
The story will be boring because I don't like this genre.
Something exciting will happen because it's a movie.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student recognizes that predictions must be supported by explicit clues from the source material.
misconceptions: This prediction is based on personal desire, not on clues from the text or visual.
This prediction is based on personal opinion, not on evidence from the text.
This prediction is a vague assumption about the genre, not based on specific evidence.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects option B, showing understanding that predictions must be based on evidence from the text/visual.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Making predictions using text/visual clues is a core reading strategy under A3.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think any plausible guess is valid, even if it lacks basis in the text or visual.

cards.question: After reading a story, you say: 'The character has already decided to run away.' This statement is an example of:
options: Inference
Prediction
Both
Neither
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding that inference draws conclusions about what is already implied, while prediction anticipates future events.
misconceptions: Prediction focuses on future outcomes. This sentence describes a decision already made, indicating inference.
The statement is about a past decision, not about a future event, so it cannot be a prediction.
The statement is a conclusion based on text clues, so it fits the definition of inference.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies the statement as an inference, showing understanding that inference focuses on past/present conclusions.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Distinguishing inference from prediction is part of using reading strategies under A3.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think inference and prediction are identical processes.

cards.question: When predicting the next scene in a film set in a rural Chinese village, which factor should you most carefully consider?
options: Your personal experience growing up in a city
Cultural practices common in rural China
Only the characters' physical appearances
A wild guess based on no evidence
cards.diagnosis: Check awareness that predictions must account for the cultural context of the text, not just the reader's own culture.
misconceptions: Personal experience is important, but it should be combined with the culture of the setting, not replace it.
Physical appearances provide clues, but cultural context helps interpret them properly.
Predictions must be evidence-based, not random guesses.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects option B, demonstrating awareness that the cultural context of the setting must be considered.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Considering cultural background is part of making informed predictions under A3.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may assume their own cultural norms universally apply, ignoring the text's cultural setting.

cards.question: Look at the image of children playing on a log in a river. Write one prediction about what might happen next. Explain how you used at least two of the three prediction factors (cultural background, personal experience, text/visual clues) to form your prediction.
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to integrate personal experience and other factors to produce a reasoned prediction.
cards.successCriteria: Student makes a plausible future prediction and explicitly references at least two of the three factors (cultural background, personal experience, text/visual clues).
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Applying the three factors to make predictions demonstrates use of reading strategies under A3.
cards.commonMisconception: Student may make a prediction without referencing personal experience, relying only on visual clues or irrelevant experience.
